newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: US donates $5 million to promote press freedom.
newsitem.headline: US donates $5 million to promote press freedom.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, laying down the law to Balkan leaders, said on Saturday that Washington would put up $5 million dollars to help ensure a free press during this year's presidential and parliamentary elections in Serbia.
She told the independent Belgrade radio station B92 that Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic faced a stark choice.
"I made very clear to President Milosevic that there is a fork in the road now, that he has the opportunity to fulfil the obligations as the president of this country," Albright said.

"That is the door for possible ways of normalising relations -- or he can put roadblocks in the way, and then, very sad for the Serbian people who have suffered enough -- they will not be allowed to rejoin the international community."
"We have pledged an extra $5 million dollars a year to make sure that it is possible now for there to be greater freedom of the press in Serbia," Albright told B92.
"That is an essential element of democratisation and an essential element of the outer wall of sanctions to be removed," she said.
She gave no indication to whom the American money would be entrusted.

Albright is on a whirlwind tour of Croatia, Serbia and Bosnia putting across the message that Washington expects The states of former Yugoslavia to keep strictly to the Dayton agreement which brought peace to Bosnia.

Milosevic seemed to have fared slightly better than his Croatian counterpart Franjo Tudjman, who got a public scolding on moral leadership, but she gave the Serbian president a long list of what he must do before his country can re-join the world community.
"First of all, there's general compliance with the Dayton accords and among those the war crimes tribunal is very important," she said.

"Then there is the whole issue of democratisation and making sure that the various aspects of democracy are able to flourish in Serbia. Obviously very high on that list is freedom of the press," Albright said.

Before meeting opposition leaders Albright made a point of giving an exclusive interview to B92 which played a vital role in massive street protests, rocking Serbia for three months last winter over election fraud.
The authorities took the radio briefly off the air but were forced to back down under immense international pressure.
